sources.name: TechRadar
sources.title: OpenAI just unveiled GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol
sources.text: OpenAI has just released a couple of brand new models to keep us on our toes. The first is GPT-6.2 Astra, designed for complex projects, and the second is GPT-6.2 Sol, designed for everyday work. Both models are available starting today in ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users. Additionally, both will be available in the OpenAI API. You won’t be able to use them from a Free account, and only in Work mode, not Chat mode. According to OpenAI, both models get better results on demanding tasks while using fewer tokens, which means you’ll get more out of your usage limits. OpenAI reports that on Agents’ Last Exam, GPT-6.2 Astra scored 5.2 points higher than GPT-6 Astra at less than a third of the estimated API cost per task and scored 5.5 points ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at just 5% of the cost. To show you what’s possible using the new model, OpenAI developer Thomas Ricouard asked GPT‑6.2 to recreate Paris at full scale so he could walk or drive through it in a browser. The model combined street maps with French survey data on more than 131,000 buildings. Thomas then explored the city and used screenshots to show the model what he wanted to change. You can explore the result yourself in Paris Atlas . I had a play with Paris Atlas, and it takes a while to load, but it is very impressive once it has. You select where on a map of Paris you’d like to walk, and it drops you onto a realistic-looking street, which you can walk around using the arrow keys on your keyboard. 3D models of various well-dressed Parisian residents walk past you on the street, and you can look all around. You actually have to navigate around the people. If you want to get a feeling of what it’s like to walk around Paris, it’s not bad at all. There’s also another change. For the first time, subscribers to the $200 per month version of ChatGPT Pro will get access to Ultrafast mode when using GPT-6.2 Sol. Ultrafast mode processes requests up to eight times faster than GPT-6 Astra in Standard mode in Codex, and was previously only available to ChatGPT Pro 500 subscribers. Pro 500 subscribers and API developers can use Ultrafast mode with either model. OpenAI says that eligible Enterprise and Edu users can access Ultrafast once their workspace admin enables it. With the ability to build impressive projects like Paris Atlas, the power of the new models is clearly quite impressive. For most people, the real question is whether any of this will make a difference to the way they use ChatGPT. Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more. If you're just asking it questions, writing emails, or generating images, probably not. But if you've ever wanted to build your own website, create an interactive tool to help you manage your finances, or turn an app idea into something you can actually use, these new models could make a real difference. Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds. Graham is the Senior Editor for AI at TechRadar. With over 25 years of experience in both online and print journalism, Graham has worked for various market-leading tech brands including Computeractive, PC Pro, iMore, MacFormat, Mac|Life, Maximum PC, and more. He specializes in reporting on everything to do with AI and has appeared on BBC TV shows like BBC One Breakfast and on Radio 4 commenting on the latest trends in tech. Graham has an honors degree in Computer Science and spends his spare time podcasting and blogging. sources.title: OpenAI anuncia GPT-6.2 Astra e Sol mais capazes e eficientes no consumo de tokens
sources.text: A OpenAI lançou o GPT-6.2 Astra e o GPT-6.2 Sol nesta terça-feira (17), novas inteligências artificiais de alto desempenho. Disponíveis para assinantes, os dois modelos são pensados para tarefas que exigem capacidade cognitiva elevada, com o Astra sendo a opção mais poderosa dentro do portfólio da empresa. São modelos de categorias distintas: o GPT-6.2 Astra é uma IA de fronteira , projetada para lidar com projetos mais ambiciosos e priorizar desempenho; o GPT-6.2 Sol é mais versátil e pensado para trabalhos cotidianos que demandam atenção adicional . No mais, ambos prometem entregar desempenho superior ao de seus antecessores, mas com menor consumo de tokens. Segundo a OpenAI, o GPT-6.2 Astra “estabelece uma nova barra de qualidade” para IA em projetos profissionais complexos . A plataforma cria slides, planilhas e documentos mais próximos dos padrões profissionais, sem tanta “cara de IA”, e segue os modelos propostos com mais fidelidade. Seus resultados em testes de benchmark foram comparados aos do GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Carbon e Claude Fable 5.2. “Treinamos o GPT-6.2 para criar slides, planilhas e documentos mais claros e bem estruturados, que seguem mais fielmente as convenções utilizadas por profissionais em áreas como direito, vendas, finanças e contabilidade”, afirma a empresa. “A redação é mais direta e específica, com menos conclusões genéricas e menos conteúdo supérfluo”, continuou. Em programação, a OpenAI afirma que o GPT-6.2 Astra é melhor em implementações e testes mais complexos em códigos preexistentes . Os testadores que experimentaram o modelo afirmam que ele escreve código mais limpo e testes mais focados, com menos rodadas de revisão. O GPT-6.2 Sol é o modelo de IA mais avançado das categorias de uso cotidiano, posicionado acima dos modelos da linha Terra . A empresa de Sam Altman afirma que o novo modelo é mais inteligente e eficiente do que o GPT-6.1 Sol, superando até mesmo o GPT-6 Astra original em determinados testes sintéticos. A OpenAI posiciona a família GPT-6.2 para concorrer diretamente com modelos de alto desempenho de rivais, comparando seus resultados em benchmarks aos do Claude Opus 5.5 e Gemini 4 Carbon — embora este último não pertença exatamente à mesma categoria. Os dois modelos foram liberados para assinantes, mas contam com mecanismos de segurança mais rigorosos para evitar o uso mal-intencionado em cibersegurança . Naturalmente, as proteções reduzem as possibilidades de uso para fins não autorizados, mas também podem limitar determinadas pesquisas legítimas. Por enquanto, os modelos da família GPT-6.2 não estão disponíveis no programa OpenAI Daybreak, que oferece as IAs com restrições reduzidas para pesquisadores autorizados. Tanto o GPT-6.2 Astra quanto o GPT-6.2 Sol estão disponíveis para assinantes dos planos ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Enterprise e Edu nos aplicativos ChatGPT Work e Codex . Os assinantes do plano Pro 500 podem ativar os modelos no modo “Ultrafast”, para processamento acelerado e maior consumo de tokens. Já os assinantes do plano Pro 200 podem ativar o modo acelerado no GPT-6.2 Sol. A OpenAI ressalta que cada tarefa no GPT-6.2 Astra “custa significativamente menos” do que no GPT-6 Astra, principalmente pela maior eficiência no consumo de tokens. Você pode conferir os resultados de benchmark divulgados no site oficial da OpenAI . Quer ficar por dentro das novidades do mundo da tecnologia? sources.title: OpenAI rolls out GPT-6.2 Astra for professional work and GPT-6.2 Sol for everyday work
sources.text: OpenAI Group PBC today announced the launch of GPT-6.2 Astra, a new frontier artificial intelligence model for complex professional work that is claimed to outperform its predecessor at less than a third of the cost, along with an updated version of its everyday model, GPT-6.2 Sol. The new models are aimed at businesses and developers looking for frontier performance at a cost that works at scale, with both said to deliver better results on demanding tasks while using fewer output tokens. According to OpenAI, GPT-6.2 Astra sets a new high on Agents’ Last Exam, a benchmark that tests multistep professional work, scoring 5.2 points higher than GPT-6 Astra while costing under a third as much. It is claimed to have finished 5.5 points ahead of Anthropic PBC’s Claude Fable 5.2 at just 5% of the cost. OpenAI is positioning GPT-6.2 Astra as the best model in the world for scientists, with the model scoring 9 percentage points higher than GPT-6 Astra on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, a benchmark for scientific work carried out in a terminal. On Harvey LAB-AA, a test of legal assignments, the model more than doubled the pass rate of Fable 5.2 at about one-sixth of the cost. Along with improved benchmark scores, GPT-6.2 Astra was trained to create slides, spreadsheets and documents that more closely follow the conventions used by professionals in fields such as law, sales, finance and accounting. The model can match a slide template from an original file or a screenshot, including layout, colors and typography down to the exact font size. Early testers of the model include accounting AI startup Basis, which said that its average time for long-horizon accounting work fell by 50%, with the time for its most complex work falling by up to 73%. Described by OpenAI as its go-to model for everyday work, GPT-6.2 Sol is claimed to let users complete more tasks on the same paid plan than GPT-6.1 Sol did. According to OpenAI, the model came within 0.5 points of GPT-6.2 Astra on Cognition AI Inc.’s FrontierCode 2.0 coding benchmark at about one-fifth of the cost. GPT-6.2 Astra comes less than two months after OpenAI called off the planned October release of GPT-6.1 Astra, after internal testing found the model fell short on staying within scope and authorization. The decision was announced the day before the company’s DevDay event in September, where GPT-6.1 Sol launched on its own. Like GPT-6 Astra, both GPT-6.2 models meet the Critical threshold for cybersecurity under OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework, and their increased capabilities have led the company to launch them with tighter safeguards for higher-risk cybersecurity assistance that are also said to restrict some legitimate vulnerability research. The company said it will work to bring the GPT-6.2 models to Daybreak , its program for vetted cyber defenders. GPT-6.2 Astra is also the first externally released OpenAI model to meet the High threshold for AI self-improvement, a measure of a model’s ability to accelerate AI research. OpenAI tracks the capability because models that help build future AI systems could outpace safeguards and human oversight, and earlier this month it disclosed Control Room , a system already deployed across its research infrastructure that can halt model output when intervention is needed. The company noted that in two of its alignment tests, the new models were more likely than GPT-6 Astra to omit mentioning obstacles that blocked their work, such as a missing file. OpenAI said it has added instructions in Codex that substantially reduce the omissions and is continuing to investigate the behavior. GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are available starting today to Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex, with Enterprise and Edu access requiring a workspace admin to enable it. Developers can also access both models through the OpenAI API. API pricing for GPT-6.2 Astra is $8 per million input tokens, 40 cents for cached input and $40 per million output tokens, a 20% discount on input and output tokens compared with GPT-6 Astra. GPT-6.2 Sol carries forward GPT-6.1 Sol’s rates of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. Support our mission to keep content open and free by engaging with theCUBE community. sources.name: The Guardian Technology
sources.title: Nvidia doubles revenue as board says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang
sources.text: Company issues first earnings report after ouster of CEO over allegations of affair with suspected Chinese spy Nvidia “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”, the chairman of the company’s board said Tuesday. Harvey Jones made the remark during Nvidia’s first quarterly earnings report since Jensen Huang’s ouster. Nvidia announced the same day that its quarterly revenue beat expectations, coming in at $115.84bn, doubling from the same time period a year ago. The third-quarter earnings report comes just days after the world’s most valuable chip company saw the ouster of Huang over allegations of several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with his own employees. Following the tumult, Nvidia’s stock tumbled more than 10%, shedding hundreds of billions in value and dropping its valuation to $3.7tn. In October, the company had hit an all-time-high valuation of nearly $6tn, but its share price has steadily fallen since then amid a broader AI slowdown. In after-hours trading on Tuesday, Nvidia’s stock ticked up 5% from earlier in the day. Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, was named interim CEO last week and delivered the financial results on Tuesday. Nvidia reported a revenue of $115.84bn and earnings of $2.68 per share, beating Wall Street’s expectations of $109.15bn in revenue and $2.47 earnings per share, according to Bloomberg analyst consensus. Nvidia’s revenue is now up 103% from the same time last year and up 20% over last quarter. “We delivered another outstanding quarter,” Kress said during an earnings call with investors. “Our ambition will not change.” When investors asked about negative effects on Nvidia’s talent retention in response to Huang’s ouster, Kress said she believed the company’s staff was “committed” and that “we will take care of our employees during this transition”. When it comes to running the business, she said “it’s business as usual”. Nvidia designs powerful computing chips used for artificial intelligence. The company controls about 90% of the chips market and the world’s top AI companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, rely on Nvidia for their technology. With much of Wall Street’s billions invested in Nvidia, the company’s twists and turns can have an outsized effect on the US economy. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and grew it from a niche firm geared toward video game chips to a trillion-dollar juggernaut at the center of the AI boom. As the CEO, he had about 60 direct reports, giving him control over most of the company’s daily functions. Last week, following reports that Huang had a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese asset, the CEO confessed to an extramarital affair. Days later, reports uncovered two more alleged affairs with company employees. On Thursday, Nvidia’s board of directors announced Huang’s resignation saying it was “effective immediately”. Donald Trump and Silicon Valley insiders, including Elon Musk, the disgraced Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick and prominent venture capitalists, have called for Huang’s reinstatement as the CEO of Nvidia. On Monday, before departing on a trip to Asia, Trump told reporters he would not mind Huang’s return: “I would not mind that … I think he learned a big lesson.” Huang issued his first public statement on Tuesday morning apologizing for his mistakes and thanking his friends and colleagues for their support. He also said he would be willing to return as CEO . “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote. Elaborating on the position that Huang would not return, Jones said that the former CEO had voluntarily stepped down and the board accepted his resignation. Jones nodded to Kress’s 13-year tenure at Nvidia, saying she has been “at the center of this company’s extraordinary growth”. “While this was an unexpected transition,” Jones said. “The board is proactively dealing with the consequences.” Huang agreed on Tuesday to appear before the House foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party and the House intelligence committee for transcribed interviews in early December. The company is also facing an investigation by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its business in China in the wake of Huang’s resignation, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday.

sources.name: Engadget
sources.title: NVIDIA's board chair says the company is not considering reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO
sources.text: Harvey Jones, NVIDIA's recently appointed board chair, joined the company's Q3 earnings call on Tuesday to comment on the resignation of Jensen Huang . Despite the former CEO floating the possibility of a potential return to his old position , Harvey quashed the possibility, saying the board was not considering reinstating Huang. Jones later said he and Colette Kress, the company's new interim CEO, would not answer any questions related to Huang. "On November 12th, our board of directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO, and board member," Jones said. "The NVIDIA board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." During the call, Kress said that the company was prioritizing its employees. "We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure that they are safe and making sure the work can be done in the current environment," she said. And while she didn't mention Huang or his resignation directly, she said that "there's also a time to think about our leadership and how important our leadership is across this organization." Mostly though, she tried to keep the call focused on NVIDIA's blockbuster quarter, saying that "from [a] business perspective, it's business as usual," for the chip giant. The statements came alongside NVIDIA's first earnings report since Huang resigned. The company easily beat investor expectations for the quarter. On Tuesday, NVIDIA said revenue increased to $115.8 billion for the three-month period ending October 25. The new number represents a 103 percent increase year-over-year from Q3 2025, and a 20 percent increase from its most recent previous quarter. Going into Tuesday, Wall Street analysts expected the company's revenue to land somewhere in the range of $109.1 billion.The company's data center revenue, which accounts for the majority of its earnings, more than doubled to $107.6 billion. Here again, the company easily beat expectations. We're likely to learn in the next day or two whether today's earnings numbers are enough to calm investors. Huang was still NVIDIA's CEO for the entirety of the company's third quarter, with Kress only holding the position for all of the past four business days. Since Huang's resignation on November 12, NVIDIA's stock had fallen about 11 percent. Ahead of Tuesday's earnings, Huang said he was willing to return to the company. "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," he wrote in a statement shared on X . Given the timing of the post, Huang's statement could be read as an attempt to pressure NVIDIA's board to give him his position back. During the call, Jones said the company's board of directors is taking the search for a new CEO "very seriously" and was considering internal and external candidates. "The board appreciates that we're living in a world where the advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are making major changes in our marketplace," he said. "Our new CEO will have to navigate those those waters very carefully, so the the the search will be thorough, and we want to install the CEO, the permanent CEO, as quickly as possible. But we won't expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person." In addition to the search for a new leader, NVIDIA will have its hands full dealing with fallout from recent revelations. According to a report The Wall Street Journal published before market close, the US Securities and Exchange Commission recently began investigating NVIDIA. The outlet said it could not immediately learn the focus of the probe. The FBI is also looking into the matter, according to President Donald Trump. If Kress is rattled by any of this, it wasn't immediately apparent in her remarks to analysts. "Our momentum is real," she said at the end of the call. "Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We've got this."

sources.title: Nvidia says it doesn’t plan to reappoint Jensen Huang as CEO
sources.text: Despite Nvidia founder and former CEO Jensen Huang’s recent offer to return to the chip company he helped build from the ground up, the company is not looking to take him back. During the company’s earnings call on Tuesday, Nvidia chairman Harvey C. Jones told listeners that Huang’s return was not something that company leadership was considering. “On November 12, our board of directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms,” Jones said, “Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO, and board member. The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” On Tuesday, Huang had posted on X that since he left the company, he has “seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” and added that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Huang resigned last week in dramatic fashion following revelations of a number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman who has been accused of being a Chinese intelligence agent. That woman, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, has maintained close ties to the former Nvidia CEO for years. Critics worry that the relationship may have influenced Nvidia’s dealings with China , and U.S. intelligence officials have expressed suspicions that she works for China’s Ministry of State Security. The development has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry at a moment when the future of the AI business, in which Nvidia plays a pivotal role, hangs in the balance. It has also spurred investigations, including an independent investigation into Huang’s activities by Nvidia’s board and an SEC probe into Nvidia . Huang has been replaced by interim CEO Colette Kress , who is also the chipmaker’s chief financial officer and executive vice president, while the board searches for a permanent replacement. Jones added Tuesday that the company was looking at both internal and external candidates. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . stories.summary: In her first earnings report as interim CEO, Nvidia's Colette Kress calmed investors' nerves, at least for the moment.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: With Jensen Huang gone, Colette Kress shows Nvidia is still at the center of AI
sources.text: Five days after Nvidia 's Jensen Huang resigned from the company he co-founded 33 years ago under a cloud of scandal, a nervous base of shareholders eagerly awaited Colette Kress' first public appearance as interim CEO. Following Nvidia's better-than-expected earnings report on Tuesday, Kress offered some relief to Wall Street, at least temporarily, by proclaiming on the call with analysts that customers are still fully onboard and that there's no slippage in demand. She said leadership from Nvidia's most important supplier, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company , visited company offices this week. "We've engaged with our customers, we've engaged with our suppliers, our partners, they're all 100% behind us," Kress said on the call. "Customers have expressed their support to the business outlook and helping us through that." While Huang was a singular figure in artificial intelligence with a commanding presence across the globe, Nvidia is still at the center of the AI ecosystem. Customers ranging from hyperscalers and neoclouds to frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic remain in persistent need of its technology and capital. Nvidia shares climbed almost 5% in extended trading on Tuesday after the chipmaker's better-than-expected earnings and strong guidance. That still leaves the stock in a deep slump after a 24% drop so far this month, driven by broad concerns about a slowdown in the AI buildout, a political handoff in Washington, D.C., and the turmoil at the top of the company. Despite all those headwinds and what Nvidia called the "unexpected transition" in leadership, the business is still booming. Revenue more than doubled in the latest quarter to $115.84 billion, and Nvidia projects roughly 90% growth in the current period to about $130 billion. More importantly, Kress said the 70% growth forecast for next year that was offered over the summer is actually too low. Now the projection is 75%. That's for a company that's seen revenue multiply by about 15-fold since the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022. While Huang is gone, "demand did not leave with him," Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives said in a note after the report. Kress maintained her optimistic tone in an interview with CNBC's Jim Cramer after the call. "The most important thing that we have been seeing is continuing growth in terms of the demand that's out there," she said. Kress also said on the call that Nvidia's stepped-up buybacks, announced in September, are still on track, confirming that the board had added $150 billion to the company's authorization for share repurchases. It's not all on Kress. The consistent message throughout the earnings call was that Nvidia is preparing for life after Huang. Harvey Jones, the newly named chair of Nvidia's board, opened by saying that Huang had resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms," the first time the board had given a reason for his removal. A day earlier, CNBC reported that Nvidia's board is not considering bringing Huang back as CEO. Kress said on the call that it's "business as usual." In a statement, she said the company's roadmap is "on track," indicating that there haven't been any changes to future chips and systems currently in development. Nvidia said that the Vera Rubin AI system is off to an "extraordinary start," selling $20 billion in the latest quarter. But Kress did signal a slight change to the company's willingness to backstop certain projects, and said Nvidia is being "disciplined" with how it's thinking about financing startups. "There's a lot of discussion internally with a lot of the teams on what we think are the best ones that we want to do," Kress told Cramer. "We're going to continue down that path to make sure we choose the right investments for us to work through going forward," Nvidia said its quarterly filing would be published in the "coming weeks," whereas it normally lands on the same day as earnings. On the call, neither Kress nor Jones addressed an avalanche of investigations and hearings in Washington looking into allegations that Nvidia was boosting revenue by selling chips to companies that are passthroughs for buyers in China. China only came up twice during the call. Kress said Nvidia had sold about $2.4 billion worth of approved data center products to China during the quarter, and that Nvidia had stopped selling licensed Hopper chips to China. Kress also noted that new trade rules released by the U.S. Commerce Department will cut off Chinese access to renting Nvidia chips. "Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us and employees are committed," Kress said when signing off the call. "We've got this." WATCH: Nvidia out with 'very solid report'

sources.name: Wired AI
sources.title: Jensen Huang Is Gone. Now What?
sources.text: I don’t go into any given week at WIRED assuming I’ll be thinking much about extramarital affairs. But last week, they were the only thing on my mind. These thoughts, of course, were prompted by Jensen Huang. In the span of a few completely insane days, the billionaire CEO and cofounder of Nvidia went from being a globally influential Silicon Valley executive to a lesson in exactly what not to do if you want to keep your job, and the extraordinary power that comes with it. It’s a damn mess—for Huang and his family, sure, but also for Nvidia, the AI industry the company is instrumental in powering, and the entirety of the global economy. WIRED’s senior correspondent Lauren Goode has spent years reporting on Nvidia and Huang, including interviewing the man himself on multiple occasions. She also spent last week breaking news about his downfall, despite being in Europe on vacation. (Sorry, Lauren. You can have those PTO days back.) So at the end of a very long week for WIRED’s newsroom, I called Lauren to talk about what she makes of Huang’s ouster, what it means for AI, and where this all goes next. We also made a bet about Huang’s future—one involving a meal he recently made semi-famous. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. KATIE DRUMMOND: Lauren, first of all, thank you for your tirelessness these past few days. The last time I saw you, we were both in Miami for WIRED’s big event , and you were getting on a red-eye that night to go to Europe for vacation, which didn’t exactly go as planned. When you saw that first story about Jensen’s affair on Sunday, what did you think? What went through your mind? LAUREN GOODE: Oof. The story first started bubbling up a while ago because The New York Times, and a lot of credit is due to The New York Times here, first reported on Nvidia’s relationship, if you want to call it that, with this company Megaspeed, back in the fall of 2025. It was a very unusual story. And for some reason it just didn’t capture the attention of people the way that more recent reporting that we and others have been doing has. Anyone who’s sort of been paying attention to that story, or had some sources in the industry, were starting to hear things. But the fact that the affair with this person, who goes by Alice Huang, was confirmed, that’s the kind of story that always captures people’s attention in a different way. There are few things people love to read about more than extramarital affairs, especially when they involve powerful people. The reason it wasn’t surprising to you, was it because of that previous reporting and what you had been hearing here and there? Or was there another reason that you saw that story and thought, “OK, actually some of this is not shocking to me”? It was both. I don’t know if you remember, Katie, but in the fall of 2024 we were doing a WIRED outing, a few of us hanging out, and we started chatting about whether or not we thought a lot of the most powerful people in Silicon Valley had girlfriends or extramarital affairs or situations. Because there are some people in Silicon Valley who are actually quite open about that. I remember us talking about it at the time, and there’s part of me that always kind of assumes that there are elements of their personal lives that we’re never going to have a full window into. Not that we were talking about Jensen that evening, but it’s always been in my mind. Then, yes, I think being on the ground in Silicon Valley, you often hear things. But a lot of times there’s a certain threshold that things have to cross in order for us as journalists to consider something reportable or something worth chasing down as reportable. I think an important distinction is that people cheat, people have affairs all the time, Silicon Valley or otherwise. What tips this over into newsworthiness is, A) the Chinese espionage of it all, and B) the affair with a subordinate. You reported that Jensen’s resignation—which really, to be clear, is the board of Nvidia ousting him—probably had more to do with the alleged affair with a subordinate than this other extramarital relationship, which is tied up in espionage allegations. A source told you this. Can you explain why that affair would tip the balance for the board? I just think it’s important to note that this doesn’t seem like it was simply a moral decision. Someone had posted on X that “I can't believe the board caved to moral pressure.” To me, this doesn’t seem like it’s a moral issue. I think if you’re looking at the three things that could have led to serious scrutiny of Jensen Huang’s behavior, there’s: One, extramarital affairs. Two, alleged extramarital affairs with subordinates within his own company. And three, an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese operative, which puts Jensen Huang in this position where the board and the investigators who are looking into this are trying to determine what he knew and when he knew it, and basically whether he was aware of the fact that chips were making their way into China. This isn’t just about the fact that someone had a girlfriend outside of their marriage. I think what is still to be revealed here could in fact be very, very serious in nature. Now, you also reported on Monday, in a fantastic scoop for WIRED , that Jensen hired a crisis comms firm a year ago. In October 2025 he hired a fixer, Risa Heller, who is very well known for working with high-profile men who are facing allegations of sexual misconduct, among other things. I’m talking about Anthony Weiner, Mario Batali, writer Jeffrey Toobin. Tell us a little bit about that story and what you found out. I really feel like with everything else going on this week, I could have gone without ever hearing about all of those stories again. Oh, you don’t want to hear about Anthony Weiner all the time? No, it turns out. I had kind of forgotten that. I was like, “I think I blocked that from my memory.” And Jeff Toobin—what a throwback. But this firm, it’s a reall

sources.title: Nvidia’s Board Has No Plans to Bring Back Jensen Huang
sources.text: As Nvidia reported its third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, the company’s financial performance was overshadowed by the drama surrounding its former CEO . And Nvidia’s board made one thing clear right off the bat: Jensen Huang isn’t coming back . At the start of the earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones emphasized the company’s strength and “groundbreaking technology” before turning to the circumstances surrounding Huang’s departure. “On November 12, our board of directors announced that, after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions … and the board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said. Asked about the company’s strategy for retaining talent and navigating the leadership transition, interim CEO Colette Kress emphasized the importance of the company’s workforce. “Our employees are absolutely instrumental to everything in this company,” Kress said. “We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure that they are safe and that the work can be done in the current environment.” Jones added that the Nvidia board is taking the search for a new CEO “very seriously” and is considering both internal and external candidates. National security dynamics are changing the chip industry, Jones said, and “our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully. So the search will be thorough. We want to install the permanent CEO as quickly as possible, but we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person.” One recurring theme emerged from the earnings call, aside from the Huang saga: Demand for Nvidia’s chips remains as strong as ever. Kress said that Nvidia expects that it will keep growing throughout 2027 and into 2028, fueled by the rise of agentic AI. Less than a week after Huang resigned as chief executive, Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue for the quarter that ended on October 25. That exceeded analysts’ expectations of roughly $109 billion and was nearly double the revenue reported in the same quarter a year ago. The vast majority of Nvidia’s revenue came from its data center business, which generated $107.6 billion, up 110 percent from a year ago. Earlier this month, The New York Times reported that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset, who had served as an executive at a Singapore-based cloud provider called Megaspeed. Then, reports emerged that Nvidia’s longtime leader additionally had an affair with one of his direct reports; following Huang’s resignation, Reuters reported he had an affair with a second employee. Huang’s relationship with the alleged Chinese operative has raised questions about what he knew about Nvidia’s advanced chips making their way into China despite US export restrictions. Nvidia had placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list in June 2025, but The New York Times reported that, according to third-party data, a subsidiary of Megaspeed “received shipments of more than $800 million of export-controlled Nvidia AI technology, including Blackwell and H200 chips,” which were subject to export restrictions. On the heels of Tuesday’s earnings, Nvidia’s stock rose in after-hours trading. The company had lost more than $1 trillion in market value over the past month amid the fallout from Huang’s scandal. Earlier on Tuesday, Huang released his first statement since his resignation. Huang thanked allies for their support, writing he’d “seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO.” He admitted to failing to “live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia,” adding that he is “committed to cooperating with the board’s independent investigation.” However, Huang concluded, if the board “decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Nvidia, which is headquartered in Santa Clara, California, has roughly 60,000 employees, and sentiments have varied in the wake of Huang’s departure. “In just three days we went from superhero cape to ‘Oops, I forgot my pants,’ and nobody’s quite sure how to swallow that,” an employee told WIRED last week. But in his 33 years leading Nvidia, Huang earned a loyal army of supporters by minimizing layoffs and red tape. Some employees have been calling for his return to the helm. And a few tech industry heavyweights are similarly eager for Huang to be reinstated. Executives including Elon Musk , Replit CEO Amjad Masad , and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan took to X to voice support for Huang, signing a petition to “Bring Jensen Back.” Huang’s activities are under investigation by at least four entities: the FBI and the US Department of Justice, Congress, the US Securities and Exchange Commission, and an independent law firm appointed by Nvidia’s board. Industry sources previously told WIRED that Huang is unlikely to return to the company anytime soon. Interim CEO Kress, at the end of Tuesday’s call, offered what sounded like a rallying cry for anyone doubting Nvidia’s future without Huang. “Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed,” Kress said. “We’ve got this.”

sources.title: Nvidia is abandoning China after Jensen Huang’s ouster
sources.text: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, acting CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country. China’s access to leading AI accelerators was an important topic during the company’s first earnings call since CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down last week. The disclosure comes the same day Nvidia announced it was creating a board-level committee to oversee national security policies , export control compliance, and global trade risks. Nvidia’s deal to sell H200 chips in China was brokered by Huang and President Donald Trump. The arrangement required the chips to be shipped through the U.S., allowing the government to collect a 25% tariff. The pathway angered China hawks who wanted to deny Chinese labs computing power and maintain the United States’ lead in AI, but Huang long argued that it was more important for the U.S. to compete in China. In April, he told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that “to concede that market for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country.” Huang’s ouster — in part over an affair with the CEO of a company under investigation for smuggling chips into China — has coincided with new rules, issued Monday, barring advanced U.S. chips from foreign data centers that serve Chinese customers remotely. Investment bank Jefferies forecast that those rules might trim between $44 billion and $62 billion from Nvidia’s data center revenue next year. Referencing the new export controls, Kress said that the backlog of demand for advanced chips like Vera Rubin means the rules would have no impact on the company’s top-line revenue. In the long term, the company may face the loss of potential customers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia. Critics of Nvidia’s dependence on China claim that as much as 20% of its revenue comes from demand linked to the country — annual revenue at its Singapore subsidiary hit $104 billion in 2025 before Nvidia stopped disclosing those figures — but that’s clearly going to change. Even before Nvidia decided to stop shipping H200s, China had largely refused to accept their delivery. The government would prefer to generate demand for the country’s domestic chip industry, even if major AI compute users want the still-superior Nvidia equipment, according to Jacob Feldgoise, a researcher at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology. Meanwhile, Chinese frontier labs are finding ways to access Nvidia chips elsewhere. All of China’s leading AI models show evidence of having been trained on Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips that are prohibited from being exported to China. That training may have taken place at data centers outside of China, but sales to those facilities will be barred under the new rules. If large data centers suited for training AI models want to buy Nvidia chips, they will have to certify they aren’t serving any Chinese customers, export control attorney Dan Fisher-Owens told TechCrunch. If they can’t provide that certification, the new rules may force them toward other chip options and further eat into Nvidia’s market share. stories.title: How to Distill Gemini Into an Edge Model
stories.summary: Turn Gemini’s annotations into an edge model for manufacturing inspection. Explore three prompting approaches, review labels, and train RF-DETR model with Roboflow. Deploy the trained model near the camera and keep Gemini available to inspect difficult cases and improve future training data.

sources.name: Roboflow
sources.title: How to Distill Gemini Into an Edge Model
sources.text: To distill Gemini into an edge model, have Gemini label your images, review and correct those labels, then train a small detector that runs next to the camera and does the routine inspections. In Roboflow, auto-label with Gemini through a class description, the Auto Label agent or an Open Prompt Workflow. Then train RF-DETR Small on the reviewed dataset, run it with Inference on your edge device, and route uncertain cases back to Gemini or a human reviewer. Checking an assembly for missing screws takes more than counting detections. A model might miss one screw and mistake a reflection for another, returning the expected count while overlooking an incomplete product. A useful inspection system needs to locate the visible screws at each mounting position and flag images that need further review. With Roboflow, you can use Gemini to help build the training dataset for that system, then train a compact RF-DETR (opens in a new tab) model to detect screws near the camera. In this approach to model distillation , Gemini generates candidate bounding boxes, you review and correct the annotations, and RF-DETR learns the specific detection task. At deployment, the smaller model handles routine detection, while routing logic sends selected difficult images to Gemini or a person for review. In this guide, you’ll explore three ways to prompt Gemini for screw annotations: class descriptions in Roboflow Auto Label, conversational feedback with the Auto Label agent, and an Open Prompt Workflow that returns boxes for inspection in Python. You’ll then review the labels, train RF-DETR Small, test it on your edge hardware, and configure a fallback for uncertain results. Before generating labels, decide exactly what one object means. In our reference image, each screw annotation covers the full visible fastener region, including its outer exposed end and inner metal feature. One screw receives one box. This definition must stay the same across the dataset. Create an Object Detection project and upload the product images (opens in a new tab) . Include complete products, missing screws, reflections, and realistic changes in lighting. In Roboflow Auto Label (opens in a new tab) , the class description is the prompt Gemini uses to find the object . Follow these steps. Gemini searches using that description, and Auto Label saves each resulting annotation as screw . The expected count of four is an application rule. It should not force the teacher to produce four boxes when a screw is missing. You can also describe the labeling task through Chat with Auto Label agent . The agent builds a labeling Workflow from the model and classes and shows a preview. Use the conversation to refine what it should label. The saved annotations still need a class name, which remains screw in this example. See labeling with the Auto Label agent (opens in a new tab) . With Gemini 4 Carbon selected, open Chat with Auto Label agent and enter the following request. Check the preview and request specific corrections. You can use the following correction when that error appears. You can also click an incorrect label or use Flag missing object. Once the preview matches the annotation rule, choose Use this Workflow, confirm the output-class mapping to screw , and select Label batch. Review the job estimate before starting. Continue with the label review in Section 2. This conversation configures the Auto Label Workflow. Gemini 4 Carbon remains the requested annotation model. Check that the saved Workflow uses it. Either setup option produces the same kind of training data for RF-DETR Small. The training examples contain reviewed screw bounding boxes. For this option, you can choose any Gemini model available in the Roboflow Google Gemini block (opens in a new tab) that supports image input and Open Prompt. You can also try different available models with the same prompt and images to compare their bounding boxes. For the Auto Label process above, Roboflow manages the saved annotations. Use the description field or the Auto Label agent conversation above. Neither option requires you to enter a JSON-format prompt or convert coordinates yourself. If you inspect raw Gemini detection output, Google's official object detection documentation (opens in a new tab) specifies box_2d in [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax] order, normalized to 0–1000. Normalization expresses a position relative to the image dimensions. A value of 500 is halfway across the relevant dimension, regardless of image size. Use the following conversion for an image of width W and height H. For example, [100, 200, 300, 250] on a 1000-pixel-wide, 600-pixel-high image gives pixel bounds xmin=200, ymin=60, xmax=250, ymax=180. This is a coordinate example, not a measured screw prediction. Prompting Gemini for boxes in a consistent format gives the visualization code a clear schema to check. Gemini models can still format their answers differently even when they receive the same instructions. This Open Prompt test uses a consistent box_2d schema and a model-independent parser. The prompt requests the screw label and [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax] coordinates normalized to 0–1000. The script accepts known JSON formatting differences, but checks the coordinates before drawing them. This follows Gemini’s object-detection coordinate convention (opens in a new tab) . The parser uses the requested coordinate order and scale. Numeric checks alone cannot prove that Gemini followed those instructions, so inspect the drawn boxes. Build this small test separately from Auto Label. Use an image input, a text input for the prompt, one Google Gemini block, and two outputs. Follow Build a Workflow (opens in a new tab) . Test with an assembly image and supply the example text in the Workflow’s prompt input. Confirm that both outputs, boxes_json and prompt_echo , appear in the test response. Save the Workflow and use Deploy (opens in a new tab) to copy its workspace slug, Workflow ID, and API URL for Python. Open Prom

sources.title: Google is making it easier to opt out of Gemini AI model training – here’s how
sources.text: You’ll soon be able to turn off Gemini model training but still retain access to your previous chats with Google’s AI. Google likes to use your conversations with Gemini for model training to help improve the AI. But for people with privacy concerns, the only way to opt out of this was to delete your entire chat history. Now, Google is overhauling the process to eliminate that drawback. Also: I checked Gemini’s new Memory summary to see what it knew about me In a change set to roll out in the coming weeks, you’ll be able to put the brakes on Gemini model training without losing access to your previous conversations with the AI. Here’s how this works now — and how it will work down the road. Currently, Gemini offers a setting called Keep Activity that controls not only whether and for how long your chats are saved but also whether they’re used to train the AI. You can’t separate the two. To correct this problem, Google will replace Keep Activity with two new settings. With the first setting, you’ll be able to keep or delete your past chats and choose how long your history will be saved. With the second setting, you’ll be able to decide whether your chats, including all text and attachments, will be used for model training. Also: I asked Gemini Notebook to ‘make me a site’ from my notes “With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training,” Google said in an announcement shared to Gemini users via email. Here’s how this will play out. If your Keep Activity setting is off when this change is made, both new settings will be off. If your Keep Activity setting is on, both new settings will be on. That means you’ll need to head to Gemini’s Settings if you wish to opt out of model training but still be able to view and access your previous chats. Almost all AIs include a setting for model training that you typically have to manually disable if you’re concerned about your privacy. But most let you opt out without turning off your chat history. ChatGPT offers a setting called “Improve the model for everyone,” which is double-speak for model training. But this is easy enough to turn off. Microsoft Copilot provides settings for “Training on conversation activity” and “Training on voice conversations,” both of which you can disable to opt out of model training. Claude’s AI training option is turned off by default. But you can always control this by checking the setting for “Help improve our AI models.” Also: 5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027 (Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.) In all those cases, you still retain access to your conversation history. In contrast, Google has been the only AI player among the majors to impose a restriction for those who want to opt out of AI training. Based on past actions, Google has often earned a reputation for being privacy-unfriendly. I’m glad to see the company take this step in the right direction. sources.name: NVIDIA
sources.title: Ian Buck Kicks Off NVIDIA’s Week at SC26 as Science Enters the Age of Agents
sources.text: NVIDIA’s Ian Buck kicked off the company’s week at SC26 in Chicago on Monday with new tools for AI agents, software that can plan experiments, run code and check results on researchers’ own systems. In NVIDIA’s special address, Buck announced Nemotron for Science , the Rubin HPC GPU and an expanded Vera CPU platform for high-performance computing . He also detailed a new collaboration in quantum computing with IBM and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory . “The frontier of computing and the new scientific stack is going to be simulation, as always, but combined with AI and the future of quantum,” said Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. Buck opened the talk by looking back to his first public talk on CUDA, at an SC06 tutorial in Tampa, Florida, 20 years ago. NVIDIA now offers more than 1,000 CUDA-X libraries , he said. “[Agents] have been just a game changer in how we interface with our supercomputers, with our devices, our instruments and how we can do the research,” Buck said. Simulation remains the foundation of scientific computing, “which will always be on the top,” Buck said, with AI, quantum and now agents working alongside it. Nemotron for Science combines the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL open model with a new open chemistry dataset and post-training recipes for life sciences and chemistry, Buck explained. Researchers can run it locally on a DGX Spark, a workstation or their own supercomputer. At Argonne National Laboratory, Buck said, an agent built with the toolkit took a single prompt, planned and tested hypotheses, chose which simulations to run and identified two new binding sites. “You own your data. You own the model,” Buck said. Buck highlighted other agents already in use: Agents lean on CPUs to run tool calls between model steps, Buck explained. “That’s exactly what agents need,” he said. “They need a CPU that can run, evaluate, run the tool, perform the operations, gather the results.” DKRZ, the German Climate Computing Center, has selected Vera CPUs for its HLRE-5 supercomputer, expected in early 2028. Buck said it joins Vera systems already announced at Texas Advanced Computing Center. Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the Vera Rubin platform, built for science, engineering, analytics and AI, Buck said. It supports precisions from FP64 to FP4, adds sparse-data acceleration and connects over seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink. With more than 50,000 CUDA cores, it has about three times as many as Hopper, Buck said. It is expected in 2028. Buck said a simulation on Jülich’s JUPITER supercomputer showed that a technique called magic state cultivation can cut the operations needed for one logical step tenfold. The work is being added to CUDA-Q. NVIDIA, IBM and Fermilab announced plans today for a quantum computing co-design platform to support error-correction and applications research. NVIDIA and IBM are pairing NVIDIA DGX B200 systems with IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk. Buck also introduced a new breakthrough for quantum decoding. The goal, Buck explained, is to cut decoding latency from about 300 microseconds to 10. A new CUDA-Q decoding algorithm, TCBP-JOBS, cuts error-correction research computation from 12 weeks to 45 minutes, he said. Buck also showed one of the first deployments of NVIDIA Photonics co-packaged optics switches, at Lambda . He said they are 15x more reliable on bit errors and link flaps. See notice regarding software product information.

sources.name: SiliconANGLE
sources.title: Nvidia at SC26: Agents are the new scientists, and they need a lab
sources.text: For most of its history, the high-performance computing market measured progress the same way: how fast a machine could solve a fixed problem. Rankings rose, a new system took the top spot, and the cycle started over. Raw performance remains the foundation of scientific computing, and Nvidia Corp. brought plenty of it to SC26. But this week, Nvidia argued that speed at solving a single problem is no longer the right way to measure leadership. An equally important question now is how many times a researcher can go from hypothesis to result in a day, and what happens when the “researcher” is an artificial intelligence agent that never sleeps. That idea ties together Nvidia’s bevy of announcements at the show. The company introduced open science models, a CPU-only supercomputing rack, a new HPC-specific GPU, a batch of CUDA-X libraries, quantum integration for the Slurm workload manager, a quantum co-design platform with IBM and Fermilab, and a co-packaged optics deployment at Lambda. It also marked CUDA’s 20th birthday. Taken individually, these announcements look like a typical supercomputing show news payload. Taken together, they describe a stack built for a different user, namely the AI agent that reasons through a scientific problem, calls a simulation, reads the result and decides what to try next. Here’s a summary of what Nvidia announced: While each announcement is interesting, the more compelling story is what they reveal about where scientific computing is headed. I see five themes. Ian Buck (pictured), Nvidia’s vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, summed up this thesis when introducing Rubin HPC: “For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery.” This marks an important industry shift. Simulation used to be the end product. In an agentic workflow, it’s a tool call within a much larger loop of hypothesis, simulation, and refinement. When an agent can generate thousands of candidate molecules or material designs, the bottleneck shifts from ideas to the time required to test them. That’s why so much of the SC26 news focuses on loop speed alongside peak flops. Nvidia says cuPhoton cut the time to correlate Event Horizon Telescope black-hole data from more than a month to eight minutes. At Pacific Fusion, a Nemotron-powered agent running on the same system can analyze plasma simulations as they run, allowing researchers to steer the simulation in real time rather than waiting for it to finish. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory is using Nvidia’s DAQIRI networking library to move electron-microscopy analysis into the experiment itself, so researchers can decide what to measure next while measurements are being taken. All of these share the same idea: Shrink the gap between asking a question and getting enough of an answer to ask a better one. For researchers, this should change how they evaluate infrastructure. Single-job time-to-solution is an important metric, but time-to-insight per iteration is equally important and should be tracked. The most important data point at SC26 may have come from a startup, not a supercomputer. Lila Sciences post-trained Nemotron with lab feedback, nearly doubling its accuracy on quantum-dot synthesis protocols to 61%, beating GPT-6 Astra’s 54% at what Nvidia states is 10 to 20 times lower inference cost. Therna nearly doubled accuracy over frontier models in predicting mRNA protein-expression ranges. Terray Therapeutics trained the model to extract reactants, products, and conditions from chemistry diagrams. That’s consistent with what I’ve been hearing across my enterprise clients: frontier models are a great starting point, but domain-tuned open models often win on accuracy and economics in specialized fields. Science pushes this further than most industries for three reasons. Research data is often proprietary or regulated. Experimental feedback serves as a training signal that general-purpose models lack. Labs want models running on infrastructure they control. That last point is why Nvidia optimized Nemotron 3.5 Super VL to run on a 128GB DGX Spark. KTH Royal Institute of Technology reports that an agent built on it fixed 81% of broken GROMACS molecular-dynamics setups in a single overnight run on a single Spark. Nvidia releasing the dataset and the recipes, not just the weights, is important here because the model is a commodity, but the know-how to adapt it is what research teams have lacked. Nvidia is well-known as the industry’s top GPU provider, but it also offers a CPU rack with Vera. Nvidia is now targeting the part of HPC that has never been accelerated, a market x86 has owned for decades. In Nvidia’s own testing, Vera delivered 1.9 times the performance and 2.4 times the performance per watt of x86 on an OpenFOAM airflow simulation. DKRZ, the German Climate Computing Center, has selected Vera for its HLRE-5 system. The new Fortran compiler beta isn’t all that sexy, but it’s an important piece. Huge amounts of scientific code are written in Fortran, and nobody wants to rewrite it. Removing that friction is how a CPU challenger takes share. Across the portfolio, Vera handles CPU-bound simulation. Rubin HPC is built for sparse, memory-bound science rather than AI training. DGX systems sit alongside IBM quantum computers. Nvidia is extending Slurm, the open-source scheduler most supercomputing centers already use, to schedule QPUs alongside CPUs and GPUs using familiar commands. Nearly 30 data centers are now deploying more than 50 quantum processors, and Alice & Bob, IBM, IQM, Pasqal and Quantinuum have adopted the expanded Slurm. Nvidia wants to be the company that coordinates whichever processor the agent needs next. An agent doing drug discovery might call a CPU-bound molecular dynamics job, a GPU-accelerated docking run, and eventually a quantum chemistry routine.
